content.title: How and When to Watch the Artemis II Crew Return to Earth
content.text: 4 min readNASA's Artemis II mission is in its final stretch, with the Orion capsule carrying four astronauts back toward Earth following a historic lunar flyby. The four-person crew—Commander Reid Wiseman, Pilot Victor Glover, and Mission Specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen—made history during the NASA’s first return to the moon since the Apollo era of the 1960s and 1970s. The 10-day mission launched on April 1 and is scheduled to conclude with a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego.Here’s what you need to know about the Artemis II mission, including when the crew is expected to return to Earth.What was the goal for the Artemis II mission?NASA//Getty ImagesNASA Mission Specialist Christina Koch looking back at Earth out of the Orion’s main cabin window.The primary objective was to test the Orion spacecraft's life support systems in deep space and verify that they can sustain astronauts on longer missions ahead. Orion consists of a crew module, which houses the astronauts, and a service module that provides propulsion, power, and life support. It is launched atop NASA’s Space Launch System rocket and is designed to travel farther from Earth than any crewed spacecraft before it. Orion is the vehicle being used for all Artemis missions.Advertisement - Continue Reading BelowThe crew is also practicing operations that will be essential for Artemis III and future missions. The broader Artemis program is aimed at establishing a sustained human presence on the moon with the construction of a lunar base. A crewed landing near the lunar south pole is planned for Artemis IV in 2028.What happened during the Artemis II flight?Since launching on April 1, the Artemis II crew’s primary objective was to accomplish a seven-hour lunar flyby using a free-return trajectory, which was the same orbital maneuver Apollo 13 relied on after its 1970 oxygen tank explosion ruled out a moon landing. (In the case of Apollo 13, however, their “slingshot” method was more of an improvisation after an explosion in one of the ship’s oxygen tanks.) In a free-return trajectory, the route uses Earth and the moon's gravitational pull to loop the spacecraft around the far side of the moon and send it back toward home without requiring significant fuel, tracing what amounts to a celestial figure-eight through space.Space Frontiers//Getty ImagesThe crew of Apollo 13, onboard the USS Iwo Jima, after their safe return. From left to right: Lunar Module Pilot Fred W. Haise, Mission Commander James A. Lovell, and Command Module Pilot John L. Swigert.In a fitting parallel, Artemis II broke the deep-space distance record set by Apollo 13 in 1970. The Orion capsule reached a maximum distance of 252,756 miles from Earth before looping behind the moon—4,101 miles farther than Apollo 13 had traveled.Jim Lovell, who led the Apollo 13 mission, died last August at age 97. But he pre-recorded a message for the Artemis II crew that they received before their departure last week. “Welcome to my old neighborhood,” Lovell said. “I’m proud to pass that torch on to you as you swing around the Moon and lay the groundwork for missions to Mars for the benefit of all. It’s a historic day, and I know how busy you’ll be. But don’t forget to enjoy the view.”NASA//Getty ImagesA view of the moon from inside the Orion module.Advertisement - Continue Reading BelowAt its closest approach, the Orion capsule flew approximately 4,067 miles above the lunar surface at 3,139 mph, with the moon described to be appearing roughly “the size of a basketball held at arm's length.” The crew spent the flyby photographing previously unseen regions of the moon’s far side and capturing images of the Apollo 12 and 14 landing sites on the near side. During this time, they were out of contact with mission control for approximately 40 minutes while behind the moon. During the flyby, the crew also witnessed a total solar eclipse as the moon blocked the sun.Perhaps the most moving moment for both the crew and people following along back on Earth was the news that the Artemis II team named a newly discovered moon crater after Wiseman’s late wife, Carroll. “We lost a loved one, her name was Carroll, the spouse of Reid, the mother of Katey and Ellie...(The crater is) a bright spot on the moon and we would like to call it Carroll,” Hansen said in a video.When will Artemis II return to Earth?RONALDO SCHEMIDT//Getty ImagesFlight controllers inside NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston.The Artemis II Orion capsule is scheduled to splash down off the coast of Southern California near San Diego at approximately 8:07 p.m. eastern/5:07 p.m. pacific on Friday, April 10. Per NASA, recovery teams will retrieve the crew by helicopter and bring them aboard the USS John P. Murtha transport dock ship, where they will undergo post-mission medical evaluations before flying back to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston.NASA will provide live coverage of the splashdown on NASA TV, the agency’s ad-free, on-demand streaming service. There’s also NASA's YouTube page, the NASA app for iOS and Android, and nasa.gov, which has been broadcasting images from Orion throughout its voyage.Rachel King (she/her) is a news writer at Town & Country. Before joining T&C, she spent nearly a decade as an editor at Fortune. Her work covering travel and lifestyle has appeared in Forbes, Observer, Robb Report, Cruise Critic, and Cool Hunting, among others. Originally from San Francisco, she lives in New York with her wife, their daughter, and a precocious labradoodle. Follow her on Instagram at @rk.passport.
